extraction_notes: Catalog is the undated (probably 2025-26) district-wide Quarry Valley Program of Studies shared by Poultney (PoHS), Proctor (PrHS) and West Rutland (WRS); no 2026-27 course list exists. Included only courses tagged PrHS, plus untagged entries (offering_note set): Survival Literature, Modern U.S. History (p.8), Lifetime Fitness, Fitness and Nutrition (.5). Courses tagged only WRS/PoHS (and "WRH" Sports & Society) skipped; no Foundations courses at PrHS. Page 3 course index lists titles with no entries in the catalog (e.g. English 1-3, Kitchen Chemistry, Guitar, Personal Fitness at PrHS) - not extracted. Graduation requirements: catalog p.2 has a two-tier table (Current vs Class of 2027+); the 2026-27 PrHS Handbook (catalogs/.../grad_requirements_2026-27.pdf, p.9) lists only the newer set as Current, which is used here. Spanish III & IV split into two records sharing a description. Some courses are listed in the catalog in a different section than their subject (Commerce and Industry under Mathematics, Health (.5) under Physical Education). Length set only where stated in prose; otherwise unknown. AP Environmental Science credits are printed "2 CREDIT". The duplicate name warning (Fitness and Nutrition x2, Health x2) is genuine: the catalog lists two distinct entries of each (different credits/descriptions).

graduation_requirements.raw_text:
QUARRY VALLEY GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS

                                                    Current
                             English - 4.0 credits (4.0 English for STC students)
                          Global Citizenship - 4.0 credits (including 1.0 U.S. History)
                                           Mathematics - 4.0 credits
                                              Science - 4.0 credits
                                        Physical Education - 2.0 credits
                                              Health - 1.0 credits
                                          Fine Art/Music - 1.0 credit
                                             Electives - 7.0 credits

                                    Total: 28 credits (27 for STC students)

                                       For Class of 2027 and Beyond
                                            English - 4.0 credits
                                       Global Citizenship - 4.0 credits
                                          Mathematics - 4.0 credits
                                            Science - 4.0 credits
                                       Physical Education - 2.0 credits
                                             Health - 1.0 credits
                                         Fine Art/Music - 1.0 credit
                                  World Language/World Culture - 1.0 credits
                                           Electives - 7.0 credits

                                               Total: 28 credits


In order for a student to earn credit in a high school level course, he/she must achieve an overall course
grade of at least 1.5. This does not apply to “Transferable Skills” which are noted with a “T.” This also does
not apply to “Habits of Work.” Upon completion of a course for high school credit, the final grade posted to a
transcript includes both proficiency and Transferable Skills grades. The final grade does not include any “Habits
of Work” grades.

courses.description: Students will be introduced to high school level proficiencies through direct instruction of texts, literary terms, and structures (both nonfiction and fiction). This course also stresses the continued improvement of writing skills with special emphasis on organization and development. This course focuses on the review of the fundamentals of grammar and usage as well as introducing a variety of literary genres such as: the short story, poetry, drama and the novel. The course is designed to teach the process skills of reading comprehension and the writing process.

Students will read diverse literature from around the world in a variety of mediums including novels, poetry, drama, short stories, non-fiction, and graphic novels. This course will focus on developing both written and oral communication skills to prepare students to engage in fluent and responsible communication and to analyze information that comes to them in many forms of expression.

American Literature will focus on critical analysis, which focuses on the standards and grade level expectations, with writing assignments designed for the students to continue their development as discriminating learners. There will be an emphasis placed on research of both primary and secondary documents. This course will include novels, plays, poems, and short stories. Writing will reflect the themes present in these works, and class discussion will revolve around thinking deeply about who we are as Americans and as individuals.

The AP English Literature and Composition course focuses on reading, analyzing, and writing about imaginative literature (fiction, poetry, drama) from various periods. Students engage in close reading and critical analysis of imaginative literature to deepen their understanding of the ways writers use language to provide both meaning and pleasure. As they read, students consider a work’s structure, style, and themes, as well as its use of figurative language, imagery, and symbolism. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. Please note that this is designed to be a fast-paced and highly demanding course. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May.

The AP English Language and Composition course focuses on the development and revision of evidence-based analytic and argumentative writing, the rhetorical analysis of nonfiction texts, and the decisions writers make as they compose and revise. Students evaluate, synthesize, and cite research to support their arguments. Additionally, they read and analyze rhetorical elements and their effects in nonfiction texts—including images as forms of text—from a range of disciplines and historical periods. Please note that this is designed to be a fast-paced and highly demanding course. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May.

courses.course_name: Creative Writing & Writing in the Workforce
courses.description: This class will focus on various elements of creative writing and literature, such as characterization, setting, plot, theme, and author’s craft. We will have the opportunity to write short stories, poems, creative nonfiction essays, and personal narratives. In this class, we will also look at famous works of creative writing and analyze them for narrative elements. The goal of “Writing for the Workforce” is to provide students an opportunity to practice communication tasks which they will most likely face upon graduating from High School. The course will also focus on professional etiquette and helpful communication strategies. Students will work individually and in groups to develop a resume, college application essay, professional emails, proposals, biographies/eulogies, letters to the editor, and other “real world” writing tasks. Students will also continue to practice their drafting and editing skills as well as explore resources they can access after graduation to improve their writing skills. The final project will be a portfolio of their revised and polished writing.

Public Speaking is designed to provide students with an abundance of opportunities to speak, in a variety of forms, in front of audiences of people. Students will read and study both vocal and body techniques that contribute to effective presentations. Reading, research, note taking and speech writing are emphasized; as well, students will explore dramatic kinds of speaking such as monologues, dialogues and other theatrical performances. The focus of the course is to provide students with opportunities to speak often and in return receive both peer and teacher feedback in an effort to help develop poised communicators.

Students who enroll in this course will get hands-on learning opportunities in trail maintenance and design. Days will be spent both inside in the regular classroom reading and writing, and outside physically engaging in lessons. In-person outdoor participation required. Students will work on trails at Pine Hill Park and take trips to research other trail systems. In the classroom, students will read literature and non-fiction about the outdoors, including modern essays, classic short stories and larger texts like Into the Wild. Text analysis, essay structure, personal reflection and formal writing pieces are central components of the course. Available to 10-12th grade students.

This course focuses on the art of the Short Story and will explore reading, analyzing, and writing short stories in a variety of genres and from a variety of different times and places. Emphasis will be placed on learning the elements of a short story (characters, setting, plot, conflict and theme) and how to manipulate each of these elements to enhance the telling of a story as well as bringing in other literary tools such as: irony, hyperbole, metaphors, simile, personification, allusion, flashbacks, symbolism, and suspense.

This course focuses on persuasive writing and speaking in order to bring about change. Students will study changemakers and what they did to accomplish change in their organizations or societies. They will learn the process of advocating for change at the school, town, state, and federal levels. Students will then choose a cause that they care about and will advocate for a positive change.

What inspires us to endure in the face of devastating and seemingly insurmountable obstacles? From survival of the human spirit to survival of the species, this course will explore fiction, non-fiction, poetry, and film to analyze and discuss the true meaning of survival. Through individual inquiry and group discussion, students will examine the writer's craft and historical context to determine the theme and purpose of each piece.

What makes movies so captivating, frightening, or eye-opening? In this course, students will analyze films/screenplays to gain a deeper understanding and appreciation for their cinematic techniques and story structures. Students will work collaboratively to critique and revise film excerpts, applying strategies related to pace, camera angles, story/character development, subtext, and more. They will then use this knowledge to create and film their own original screenplay(s).

Civics will examine what it means to be an American. Students will learn about the foundations of the American political system, and what values and principles are basic to American constitutional democracy. Students will learn about the relationship we as citizens have with our government and will examine the rights and responsibilities of citizens. The course also examines the structure of the U.S. government and how it functions.

Global Studies will examine world history, world cultures, and international relations from the 1400s into modern times. Emphasis will be placed on current events as they relate to historical events. This course is designed to give students opportunities to learn about our increasingly interdependent world.

U.S. History is a survey of US history from the Civil War era to modern times. Topics may include industrialization, immigration, globalization, war and peace, civil rights and significant political, socioeconomic, and cultural developments in the U.S. since the Civil War.

The AP U.S. History course focuses on developing students’ understanding of American history from approximately 1491 to the present. The course has students investigate the content of U.S. history for significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods, and develop and use the same thinking skills and methods (analyzing primary and secondary sources, making historical comparisons, chronological reasoning, and argumentation) employed by historians when they study the past. The course also provides seven themes (American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and environment; and culture and society) that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May. Prerequisites: Students must have completed Civics and Global Studies with a passing grade.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed Civics and Global Studies with a passing grade.

courses.description: Intro to Psychology is designed to help students understand the varied topic of psychology. This course will introduce topics such as learning, memory, sensation, perception, personality development, behavior, and abnormal psychology. Historical and contemporary research techniques as well as important historical figures in the field of psychology will also be a focus.

Current Events is a daily news reading course where students will hone the skills that are needed to become an informed consumer of the news. Each week students will be engaging in a variety of activities revolving around the news of the day. Class objectives include such things as differentiating news media and other types of media, examining the nature of local news, and building awareness of current events outside of the United states. Units of study will include such things as Identifying Media Bias, Understanding Demographics, and Conflict.

We all possess a vast array of knowledge surrounding our social identities, how social relationships are organized, and how groups and institutions operate. However, our study of sociology will reveal that we all carry misconceptions about the world in which we live. Thus, it becomes our goal during this semester to discover, to deconstruct, and to question those things in society that we often take for granted.Together we will discover the complexities of our society. The goal is for us to work within sociology as a science, dealing with the hows and whys of asking sociological questions, and how to coordinate sociological research. Once we have approached sociology as a science we will examine several different areas of sociological study. These include culture, social structures and deviance, social inequality and class, racial inequality, gender inequality, work, education, mass media, and health.

Modern U.S. History explores the key events and cultural shifts in the United States since 1945. This engaging class examines post-World War II society, the Cold War, U.S. foreign relations, the Korean and Vietnam Wars, the impactful social and political movements of the 1960s, and America's involvement in the Middle East. We will also discuss the ongoing divide between liberalism and conservatism and the evolution of contemporary American culture. Join us to uncover the compelling stories that have shaped modern America.
courses.notes: Catalog also lists a different Modern US History (PoHS) on p.7; this entry (p.8) has no school tag

courses.description: Have you ever found yourself relating to Peter Parker, a.k.a. Spider-Man? Or contemplated the significance of Superman’s declaration, “I fight for truth, justice, and the American way”? If these thought-provoking questions resonate with you, join us for Comics & Culture, where we will dive deep into the profound impact that comic books, and other comic related materials, have had on our society. Together, we will investigate how comics confront critical issues—such as identity, race, politics, representation, and social justice—while examining their lasting impact on cultural norms and political discourse. Don’t miss out on this engaging journey into the world of comics and their transformative power! Alongside Comics & Culture, students will learn how to create their own characters as well as how to visually tell a story in Character Design & Illustration! We will look at how artists use illustration to communicate visual metaphors. By the end of the course students will have their very own comic written and illustrated by them!
courses.notes: School tag: PrHS; Listed in Global Citizenship section; half Art credit, half Social Studies credit

courses.description: In the course "Sports and Society," students will explore the vital role that sports play in shaping global cultures. We will examine how sports reflect societal values and movements, giving athletes and fans a platform for cultural expression. While the course will cover various sports worldwide, the primary focus will be on American sports and their societal impact. At times, students will have opportunities to take charge of their learning by choosing projects that demonstrate their understanding of a unit's objectives. Key topics will include Sports Reflecting Culture, Representation and Social Change, and the Rise of Women’s Sports, offering an engaging and relevant educational experience.

Algebra 1 begins with a basic review of order of operations, ratios, and proportions leading into the topic of Observed and Theoretical Probability. Students will study the different forms of linear equations, intercept form, standard form, and point-slope form and apply the various forms to real world applications. Students will study systems of linear equations and systems of inequalities with the focus on graphing, substitution and elimination methods with an introduction to matrices. Students will study exponents and exponential equations involving exponential growth and decay. Students will study rational functions; linear, exponential, and quadratic. The focus toward the end of the course will be working with polynomials, multiplying and factoring, the zero product property, and roots of quadratic equations.

A study of Mathematics that begins with undefined and defined terms. Students use the undefined and defined terms throughout the course to build a basic understanding of mathematical systems. Students study the topics of inductive and deductive reasoning, congruence of polygons, similarity of geometric figures, properties of circles, area of regular and complex geometric figures as well as the volume of geometric solids. Students explore the geometric concepts throughout the course using classical construction tools, the compass and straightedge. Students will also use their knowledge of Algebra to study aspects of coordinate geometry, the Pythagorean Theorem, and introductory trigonometry.

In this course students’ understanding of prior algebra skills and concepts will be extended to include topics essential to a second year course. Topics include recursion, data analysis, linear systems, functions, transformations, exponents and logarithms, polynomial functions, conic sections, rational functions, and trigonometry. Graphing calculators and appropriate technology will be used to enhance understanding and extend exploration in many areas. This course is open to all students who have successfully completed proficiencies in Algebra I and Geometry.

This course emphasizes basic trigonometry concepts, equations, identities, graphs, inverse relations, complex numbers, polar coordinates and applied problems in the first semester. In the second semester topics covered include conic sections, logarithms and exponents, sequences and series, limits and some probability and statistics if time permits. In addition to creating a basic understanding of these topics, the course will also lay a foundation for Calculus or other advanced mathematics courses students may encounter in college.

Understanding financial management concepts is an important life skill. From credit to insurance to taxes, it is imperative that students understand the consequences of their choices. A thorough understanding of financial concepts, with practical application through activities and projects, will enable students to leave this course with applicable useful skills for life. This course surveys the basic personal financial needs of most individuals and emphasizes the basics of budgeting, saving, checking, debt, consumer awareness, investments and credit. Students will build strong money habits early on and avoid many of the mistakes that lead to lifelong money struggles.

American Entrepreneurship is a course designed to help students gain an understanding of how to start and successfully run a small business and develop the skills necessary to be an entrepreneur and run a business. Topics covered include entrepreneurship, management, advertising, market research, financial planning and the legal aspects of starting a small business. Hands on projects, group activities and guest speakers from area businesses will support the learning process.
courses.notes: School tag: PrHS; Listed at end of Mathematics section

courses.description: Earth Science is the first high school course in science. Earth Science is the study of the world around you. In this course, students will study earth, both as it exists by itself, and as part of the solar system. Topics and themes include the structure of the earth, astronomy, the atmosphere, weather, climate, geology, and the impacts humans have on the planet. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations.

Biology is the scientific study of living organisms. Students participating in this course will develop an understanding of the principles of biology including, lab safety, scientific processes, ecology, cells, genetics, evolution and the six kingdoms. The course considers the interactions among the vast number of organisms that inhabit planet Earth. It presents the basic form and function of these organisms, from cells to organ systems, and simple to complex cellular structure. It delves into interactions between organisms, and between an organism and its environment. Laboratory work, hands-on activities and some dissections will help students on their journey through the amazing living world. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations.

Chemistry is the study of the composition and properties of substances, and the changes that such substances can undergo. Students will explore the fundamental principles of chemistry which characterize the properties of matter and how it reacts. Topics may include, but are not limited to: measurement, atomic structure, electron configuration, the periodic table bonding, gas laws, properties of liquids and solids, solutions, stoichiometry, reactions, kinetics, equilibrium, and acids and bases. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations. To be successful at the Honors level work, students should have strong algebra and proportional reasoning skills. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Earth Science, Algebra I and Geometry or instructor permission.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed Earth Science, Algebra I and Geometry or instructor permission.

courses.description: Forensic Science I is designed to introduce students to key concepts and methods of forensic science, more commonly known as crime-scene investigation. To be successful in this course, students should be working toward meeting proficiency in Biology. Forensic Science is designed to introduce students to key concepts and methods of forensic science, more commonly known as crime-scene investigation. This course will include the following units of study: observation skills, evidence collection, death, fingerprints, DNA fingerprinting, blood and blood spatter, hair, fibers and textiles, pollen and spores, toxicology, handwriting analysis, soil, glass, forensic anthropology, casts and impressions, tool marks, and ballistics. This is a fast-paced hands-on course with frequent laboratory exercises embedded into class time. Prerequisite: Students must have completed or be enrolled in Biology.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed or be enrolled in Biology.

courses.description: In this course, students will study the structure and function of the human body in detail. In addition to a survey of all major human organ systems, classroom activities may include the dissection of various animal organs. This is an advanced science class with many aspects that mimic a college-level course including significant out-of-class study and review. To be successful in this course, students should have met proficiency in Biology. Available to 11-12th grade students.

This course is an introduction to the major topics in Astronomy, such as: light and matter, space and time, planets, stars, galaxies, and the universe. Hands-on and computer-simulated activities are included to gain laboratory experience within the regular course time. Outdoor night-time observations of the sky are also strongly encouraged.

This is a course to introduce students to the engineering design process, which is an iterative, problem-solving cycle. Students will experience this process through a series of hands-on engineering design challenges. Throughout the course, students will study and design within the four major branches of engineering: civil, mechanical, electrical, and chemical.

This course is designed to provide a clear and straightforward presentation of the basic concepts of physics. The central theme, the interrelationship between matter and energy, applies to all sciences. Major topics in physics will be studied, such as: motion, forces, gravity, and energy, states of matter, waves (sound and light), static and current electricity, magnetism, and modern physics (including relativity and quantum mechanics). Mathematical connections and problem solving will be highly emphasized in this course. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors credit, with increased expectations. To be successful in this course students should have met proficiency in Algebra I and Geometry. Available to 11-12th grade students.

To be successful in this course, students should have met proficiency in Chemistry. AP Biology will cover the biological processes of the living world in great detail. Its content will emphasize the four big ideas of biology: (1) the process of evolution drives the diversity and unity of life, (2) biological systems utilize free energy and molecular building blocks to grow, to reproduce, and to maintain dynamic homeostasis, (3) living system store, retrieve, transmit, and respond to information essential to life processes, and (4) biological systems interact, and these systems and their interactions possess complex properties. Students electing this course should be aware of additional out of class reading and study, as would be found with a typical biology college course. This is a laboratory course. Students will have an extra lab period(s) each week. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May.

To be successful in this course, students should have met proficiency in Biology and be co-enrolled in chemistry. The AP Environmental Science course is designed to be the equivalent of a one-semester, introductory college course in environmental science, through which students engage with the scientific principles, concepts, and methodologies required to understand the interrelationships of the natural world. The course requires that students identify and analyze natural and human-made environmental problems, evaluate the relative risks associated with these problems, and examine alternative solutions for resolving or preventing them. Environmental Science is interdisciplinary, embracing topics from geology, biology, environmental studies, environmental science, chemistry, and geography. This course includes a required lab and prepares students to take the College Board’s AP Environmental Science exam in May. Available to 10-12th grade students.

In this course, students will study principles of electricity in depth as they work with concepts of voltage, resistance, current, and capacitance, build complex circuits, study renewable energy, and work with robotics. Topics included may depend on time and student interest. This is a hands-on, project based course with significant time spent in the lab.

This course covers makerspaces and making activities to support inquiry-driven and community learning in information institutions. Resources, facilitation, and learning around communities and practices of making are examined. Students gain hands-on experience with digital and physical making toolkits and design and develop a makerspace-related learning environment within an information institution.

Marine biology is the study of organisms in the ocean and the physical and chemical properties of the ocean that influence underwater life. This is an introductory course with many hands-on activities. Topics of study include the seafloor, seawater and the world ocean, basics of biology, marine life, and marine ecosystems.

This course encompasses the development and use of medical vocabulary, definitions, and medical abbreviations. Students will build medical terms through the use of prefixes, word roots, combining forms, and suffixes.

Students in physical education classes follow a structured curriculum focusing on two areas: individual/team sports and introduction to fitness. The individual/team sports curriculum includes a variety of activities designed to enhance self-confidence, group dynamics, and coordination and movement skills. The introduction to fitness curriculum focuses on the five components of fitness, instructing students in the basics of exercise physiology and providing insight into the importance of life-time activities. Students are assessed on their ability to successfully complete required activities and class projects. Teachers use a grading rubric to help students understand expectations and track performance. As in all physical education classes, each student will be evaluated on participation, attitude, projects and/or written tests.

These 3 standards will be the focus for this class: 1.Selects and participates in physical activities (e.g., dance, yoga, aerobics) that meet the need for self-expression. 2.Applies knowledge of movement sequences to create or participate in one or more forms of dance. 3.Demonstrates appropriate technique in flexibility training. In this class we will practice mobility routines to increase our flexibility. Self expression will be explored by researching dance genres, choreographing short dances, practicing several yoga methods, engaging in pilates and imagery. Come try these lifetime fitness activities so you can grow your knowledge and tap into the benefits of each. This physical education class performs various types of workouts three days a week. Students will learn to self-monitor through reflections, informal daily check-in, producing a wellness portfolio and MyPlate guidelines. Students will develop a fitness and nutrition plan and have the semester to try to work towards and achieve these goals. The goal of this course is to allow students to investigate issues affecting their health in today's society.

3 standards the whole class will be based around: 1.Selects and participates in physical activities (e.g., dance, yoga, aerobics) that meet the need for self-expression. 2.Applies knowledge of movement sequences to create or participate in one or more forms of dance. 3.Demonstrates appropriate technique in flexibility training. In this class we will practice mobility routines to increase our flexibility. Self expression will be explored by researching dance genres, choreographing short dances, practicing several yoga methods, engaging in pilates and imagery. Come try these lifetime fitness activities so you can grow your knowledge and tap into the benefits of each.

Students learn about the health related fitness components, healthy lifestyles, nutrition and other aspects of health and wellness. This physical education class performs various types of workouts three days a week. Students will learn to self-monitor through reflections, self-assessing and producing a wellness portfolio. Students will develop a fitness and nutrition plan and have the semester to try to work towards and achieve these goals. The goal of this course is to allow students to investigate topics around fitness and wellness in today's society while being able to work towards current health goals.
courses.notes: Second, untagged Fitness and Nutrition entry (.5 credit); a PrHS 1-credit entry also exists

courses.description: Students learn about the health related components, body fat percentage norms, nutrition and other aspects of health and wellness. This course is designed to expose students to information and trends affecting teen health and is based on the National Health Education Standards. Health literacy subjects will include: using the internet to access health information wisely and safely, the effect of media in today's world, decision making/goal setting and refusal skills in relation to the difficult decisions teens make in today's world, communication skills, relationships and relationship abuse, societal roles and issues, sexual safety and reproductive health. This class is based on group and individual exploration as well as readings, lecture and media presentations. There will be projects and/or presentations in a peer to peer teaching format for concepts and ideas important to teens. Use of media based presentations or visual and oral presentations and reports will be made individually and as a group. Class participation is extremely important.
courses.notes: School tag: PrHS; Listed at the end of the Physical Education section; a separate 1-credit Health course is listed under Health

courses.description: Emphasis in this course will be on muscular strength, muscular endurance, mobility, safety and principles of fitness. Students will perform a variety of workouts and activities done throughout the semester that will contribute to the development of an intense repertoire of various exercises. Topics will contain but not be limited to the following: physiology of the cardiovascular system, anatomy of muscles, correct lifting techniques, group/personal fitness, benefits of participation in such programs and designing a personal fitness program.

To build students' health knowledge and skills development in an effort to prepare and empower students to value and engage in healthy lifestyles. The course content includes: body structure, human growth and development, family and mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, safety, personal health habits, drugs and alcohol. The skills that will be developed in this class are: decision making, communication skills, examination of values and attitudes, location and evaluation of health related information, application and coping skills.

This course will help you develop your artistic vision and release your creative potential! Painting introduces basic watercolor, and acrylic principles and techniques with an opportunity for multimedia endeavors. Students learn the various forms of composition: still life, landscape, and portraiture. Students will paint at least 5 paintings covering a wide range of themes and styles.

This course is intended for students who have previously taken Painting 1 and are looking to further their knowledge and practice in painting. Students will engage in a more rigorous independent study of drawing and painting with a focus on developing technical as well as conceptual skills. Students are encouraged to explore multimedia work and incorporate various techniques into their work.

This course is intended for those studying ceramics for the first time (or more than once) and is a comprehensive introduction to the craft of clay working. The primary emphasis is on studio work leading to a portfolio of finished pieces by the end of the semester. In addition to demonstrations of technique and technical assignments, you should take a field trip to view historic and contemporary examples of fine ceramic art. Periodically throughout the term, I will show slides or films to help illustrate what you are learning. The main goal of this course is that you will be able to create as well as appreciate expressive, beautiful three dimensional clay forms. You will have an understanding of other cultures and periods of human expression in clay and finally you will begin to be proficient at forming clay objects yourself.

This course will utilize Adobe Photoshop and Illustrator to take your creative ideas online! In an increasingly digital sphere students will have the opportunity to use professional programs to create digital images that are completely unique. No camera? No problem, students can use their cellphones OR one of our DSLR cameras at school!

This foundation course is recommended for students with an interest in ceramics, sculpture, printmaking, and various applied arts. Why not try it all? Design and create art objects using a variety of materials.As students continue to develop their own skills, they will explore how people through the ages expressed themselves through traditional and contemporary crafts, making both functional and decorative pieces.

This course is intended to build upon skills and practice covered in Studio Art Review. Students who have previously taken Art Review will continue their practice with conceptualizing ideas and creating visual representations. Students are encouraged to independently research and develop themes in their work while experimenting with various materials. This is a great introduction for students who are interested in pursuing AP Studio Art.

This course delves into the practice of printmaking, its application, and how it can be manipulated into a fine art form. We will also fine tune drawing skills as they are essential in this practice. Students will explore etching, silkscreen, monoprint, collagraph, woodblock, and linocut prints. We will look at printing on various surfaces and textures including t-shirts, tote bags, fabrics, and paper.

This class explores all three-dimensional areas of art utilizing traditional sculpture, architectural models, apparel, ceramics, stone carving, or wood works. Artwork will range from realistic to abstract. This art course deals with art in its 3-dimensional form. A variety of mediums will be explored, which may include textiles, ceramics, paper mache’, wire sculpture...and more!

This course will teach students how to design, plan, and build scenery and props for theater productions. Students will act as professional stage hands, working directly with the theater directors to bring the vision of the show to life. Students will learn how to plan and budget for materials, how to work as a team to bring a creative vision to life, as well as the history of theater and how different sets affect a show.

Students create a portfolio of work to demonstrate inquiry through art and design and development of materials, processes, and ideas over the course of a year. Portfolios include works of art and design, process documentation, and written information about the work presented. In May, students submit portfolios for evaluation based on specific criteria, which include skillful synthesis of materials, processes, and ideas and sustained investigation through practice, experimentation, and revision, guided by questions. Students may choose to submit any or all of the AP Portfolio Exams.

Open to any students with at least one year playing experience or permission from the teacher. High School Concert Band is a performing ensemble that focuses on the ability to create music on a band instrument. Students in this course will build upon the technical skills learned in Middle School Concert Band through a variety of different genres of music. The goal of this course is to use these techniques to develop both personal and ensemble skills as well as discover how to use these skills to connect the technical and emotional aspects of music. Students will be required to play for a variety of performances throughout the year which may include the following: the Rutland Halloween Parade, the Loyalty Day Parade, the Vermont All State Parade, the Memorial Day Parade, the Winter Concert, Arts Night, and the Spring Concert. Students will also be required to help with the Green Mountain District V High School Auditions which are normally hosted at PrHS every year. Students have the opportunity to audition for the Green Mountain District V High School Music Festival.

Students enrolled in this course will learn the basics to playing ukulele including, how to play written melodies (plucking) and how to play chords to accompany a sung song. A variety of genres will be used to accomplish this including popular songs and Hawaiian songs. Students will discover Hawaiian culture and how the ukulele is used to represent aspects of that culture. Students will learn how the ukulele is incorporated into reggae music and compare and contrast Hawaiian and Caribbean reggae. Instruments are provided by the school. Students will be required to perform within the classroom and/or record themselves.

Students enrolled in this dual enrollment course will be introduced to the music of a variety of cultures from around the world. Some cultures may include: Chinese, Japanese, Indian, Native American, Sub-Saharan African, Indonesian, Pacific Island, and European. Students will learn how music in these cultures evolved, what makes each genre unique, how music is used in each culture, as well as recognize and describe the characteristics of each genre. Depending on class size and available funds, the students may go on field trips to see Global Music performances.

Students will learn to understand spoken Spanish using vocabulary and constructions appropriate for the earliest phases of language learning. Students work toward proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, writing, and cultural competency. Students will be able to answer questions, and ask these questions in the appropriate situations. Students will follow and carry on basic conversations using familiar construction and vocabulary. Students will read and write all material learned orally. Countries in which Spanish is spoken will be culturally explored.

Students will review and expand upon vocabulary and constructions previously studied. Class activities will be conducted increasingly in Spanish, and students are expected to actively participate, utilizing the language as much as possible. Reading and writing skills will be developed. Works in Spanish will be read. Cultural elements and current events will be explored. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Spanish I

Students will continue to review and develop vocabulary and learn more complex structures and concepts inherent to Spanish language and culture. Students will speak Spanish in class. Journal writing and individual language projects will be emphasized. Literature will continue to be explored and additional works read. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Spanish I & Spanish II. To take Spanish IV, Spanish III must be successfully completed.

courses.description: The AP® Spanish Language and Culture course develops language and cultural proficiency at the Intermediate to Advanced level. Students and the teacher commit to using Spanish as the language for communicating about the course content and for social classroom interaction. Regular use of Spanish in the classroom is assessed as a component of evidence of interpersonal speaking proficiency. The course is taught through engaging with authentic resources from across the Spanish-speaking world. By interacting with these sources in Spanish, students develop the language knowledge and communication strategies to interpret texts and to acquire knowledge of cultural products and practices and reflect on underlying perspectives.

In this course, students travel the Spanish-speaking world, looking at how the culture and geography of a country, as well as its political and agricultural landscape, shape how, why, where, when, and by whom food is made and consumed. Students participate in online explorations and activities, as well as self-designed projects, showcasing their cultural and culinary learning. Field trips to various locations and/or guest presenters help enrich students’ understanding of the content being studied. Cooking experiences will take place several times during the course, both in and outside of the classroom.

Get ready for an exciting journey into the world of plants! In this year-long horticulture course, you'll dive into the fascinating science of growing plants. We’ll kick things off by exploring your thoughts about food, discovering where it comes from, and tracing the incredible journeys it takes to reach our region.As we move forward, you'll learn all about the science behind plant growth and reproduction. The highlight? You’ll have the chance to cultivate your own seedlings in our greenhouse, which will later bloom in our school and community gardens come spring. Imagine watching your hard work transform into beautiful plants that benefit those around us! But that's not all! This course will also open your eyes to various hobbies and exciting careers in horticulture and agriculture. You’ll engage in both group and independent projects that will challenge your creativity and teamwork skills. Plus, expect fun quizzes and thought-provoking papers along the way!And let’s not forget the best part—get ready to spend plenty of time outdoors in our greenhouse, where you'll connect with nature and see firsthand the magic of plant life. Join us for a year of growth, learning, and adventure in horticulture!

Members of Yearbook staff will work to become proficient in the practical and ethical skills needed to design and construct the Proctorian such as interviewing, digital photography, layout and design, budgeting, sales and marketing. They will become capable of properly operating digital cameras and photo applications while having exposure to various types of technology such as Chromebooks, desktops, personal devices and computer software programs such as Photoshop and Yearbook Avenue. Working both individually and collaboratively as they move through the creative process, students will be assessed by targeting the Transferable Skills.

Student enrollment in Driver’s Education is limited to 20 students per class, and selection will be prioritized by student’s date of birth. A student must have a valid Vermont Learner’s permit on the first day of class. A proficiency grade will be issued for driver’s education. This course consists of five parts: ● Classroom component (at least 30 hours) which may be conducted in-person or remotely. ● Behind the wheel component (at least 6 hours), The B-T-W and observation time is done in the Driver education vehicle. ● Observation component (at least 6 hours) ● Parent/Guardian component (practice driving time). Parent component is 40 hours of supervised practice driving time of which 25 hours is during student enrollment in the Driver Education Course. ● Social Responsibility component (student’s attitudes and behaviors). Students are expected to follow appropriate GRCSU Health and Safety Guidelines, demonstrate self-respect to themselves and others, think before they act, accept responsibility for their actions, participate in group discussions and follow the rules in the school setting and outside on the road. If minimum attendance requirements are not met, the student will be dropped from the course. How is a student assessed? (Learning Target/Course Assessments) ● In the classroom phase, the student must score at least proficient on each unit discussed, and score at least 80 on the final exam. ● Students must show they are responsible citizens with socially responsible attitudes and behaviors. Attitudes and behaviors will have a bearing on whether students will receive a Driver Education Completion Certificate. ● In the driving phase, the student will have a driving route to practice various techniques and skills. ● Students will be given a mock final road test for their final drive. They must score at least 80% proficiency on the Driver Education Final Road Test. ● Parents will be required to attend a parent meeting or schedule an initial check-in meeting with the instructor. What will Driver Education students learn? (Enduring Understanding/Indicators) The classroom has nine units of knowledge and understanding. It includes but is not limited to the following: Getting ready to drive, understanding driver vehicle readiness, laws of the road, basic driving, maneuvers (parallel park, VT Turnaround, and hill start), managing risks, time and space, rural and city driving, interstate driving, impaired driving, distracted driving, use of the safety systems, physics and car crashes, biology and car crashes, adverse conditions, environmental issues, insurance, basic car and tire maintenance, and trip planning.

courses.course_name: Career Exploration and Post Secondary Planning
courses.description: This course is the second half of Drivers Ed. In Career Exploration, students will take a look at various post secondary opportunities, career options and how their personal interests, aptitudes, and values fit into the overall picture of choosing a fitting career. The students will have an opportunity to see different college and career paths, and talk to speakers to gain a better understanding as to how they can take their education and transition into a career opportunity. Students will also take a look at goal-setting and the decision making process in order to better understand how decisions we make today can affect our futures. During this quarter course students will: ● Explore post secondary planning, careers, and paths that will lead them to make the right choices towards their future ● Have the opportunity to talk to professionals both in and outside of the classroom ● Take field trips to enhance their understand of different post secondary opportunities, college, careers, and professions ● Complete a research project based on one career of interest Students will demonstrate their understanding of different careers during a community based presentation at the end of the quarter where they will present their findings to the elementary school.
